fixes.explanation: That's the opening line. The LORD says, “I have heard your prayer…” (2 Chronicles 7:12). Solomon, Israel's king, had prayed at the temple, and the first thing he hears is that he was heard. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, friend, so I can tell you that hits different.

I see why a king and a building project make that tempting. But the LORD doesn't call this a house of kings. He says He has chosen this place “…as a house of sacrifice.” The palace is Solomon's own project, and the temple is the one the LORD names for Himself.

Treasure sounds right for a building that big, friend. I'd have guessed it too, and then I'd have tried to stamp it on a cookie. But the LORD says He has chosen this place “…as a house of sacrifice.” Not a vault, not a showroom. A house where sacrifice is offered, and that's the label He gives it.

Reaching out for help is a natural instinct. It's the same one that makes you text the group chat before you read the instructions. But the LORD never says to call on the king. The people He speaks of are the ones called by His name, and they humble themselves, pray, seek His face and turn from their wicked ways (2 Chronicles 7:14).

Heal is right. The LORD says, “…then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.” That's three promises in one sentence. He has just talked about the sky closing, locusts or a plague, so I think a land in trouble would be glad to hear it (2 Chronicles 7:13).

A land in trouble needs a hug, not a flood, friend. The LORD says He will “…hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.” Healing is the word He uses. And the hard times before it, no rain, locusts or a plague, are things He says might come (2 Chronicles 7:13).

True. The LORD says, “My eyes and My heart will be there for all time.” He also says He has chosen and consecrated this temple so that His Name may be there forever (2 Chronicles 7:16). Solomon, Israel's king, heard this at night, once the temple and palace were finished. That's a promise worth hearing twice.

Throne it is. The LORD says, “…then I will establish your royal throne, as I covenanted with your father David…” David was Solomon's father and king of Israel before him (1 Kings 2:12). The promise comes with a condition: Solomon walks before the LORD as David walked. I bet that's a lot of pressure for one man.

An army is a natural thing to picture for a king, and it would look great on a cookie. But the LORD never mentions one here. He says, “…then I will establish your royal throne…” (2 Chronicles 7:18). The promise is about the seat of the king himself, tied to the covenant with his father David, so that's the word for the blank.

The text says the opposite. The LORD says, “And when this temple has become a heap of rubble, all who pass by it will be appalled and say, ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this land and to this temple?’” (2 Chronicles 7:21). They'd be appalled, and they'd ask about it. I think this is one of the heavy lines in the passage.
